I'm at a AI-for-physics workshop. I think one thing which has become stark is that as more and more people start using LLMs and other AI agents, it is something we will have to embrace.

One of my issues with the current use of LLMs is that they make the review process harder, not easier. This is contrary to general expectation with LLMs - in general one assumes that they make peoples lives easier. I think the problem is that when people use them to write Lean code, the general use case is to make the life of the author easier not the reviewer. This, naturally, in the end makes it harder for everyone in the long run.

I was therefore thinking that we could put together a list (or skill? - if that is the correct use case) of things we want the LLMs to do which would make the review process a lot easier.

This is some stuff I had in mind, but open to suggestions:

  • Split your pull request into lots of small commits, all of which build, and all of which have a descriptive title.
  • Make sure you do not replicate any lemmas which already exist.
  • Make sure results sit in the correct file with library building in mind.
  • Write good documentation similar to this file.
  • In your PR description, give a list of the lemmas and definitions added or removed, what file they are in, and a short explanation of what they do.
  • Make sure long proofs are split into smaller lemmas.
  • Be prepared to have a back and forth in the review process.

I can add the following (from your project side):

  • document your review standards - including style guidelines. (If you discover implicit undocumented mathlib conventions you're following, we'll happily take PRs also.)
  • add an explicit AI policy,
  • make it say that PRs not meeting your quality bar may be closed without comment (when too low-value).

Make sure you do not use any lemmas which already exist.

Is there an additional negation? I would have said the opposite :-)

Michael Rothgang said:

Make sure you do not use any lemmas which already exist.

Is there an additional negation? I would have said the opposite :-)

Fixed :).
A first pass at an AI policy which takes what I've written above into account is at Physlib#1149. Any comments are very much appreciated here. (Thanks to @Shlok Vaibhav for relevant discussions)

Thanks, looks like a good start! Some comments --- some about clarification of what you're writing, some about edge cases you may want to consider:

  • "split into small commits": do you mean atomic commits? Is one commit for the entire PR ok? Is a huge PR ok if it splits into many little commits? (My take: PRs should not be too large; please use atomic commits when sensible. Mathlib is not strict about this, and squashes PRs upon merge.)
  • "commits should build" --- you mean "each individually" (i.e., atomic commits)?
  • are there consequences if a PR author uses LLMs to respond to the author (for example)? For instance, would you like to reserve the right to insta-close the PR and not accept it?
  • in general, what will you do with PRs that fail to meet some requirements below (such as, not disclosing AI use) that are not obviously technically bogus?
  • there should be a good PR description. This includes no superfluous AI waffling ("Test plan" which is just lake build/a subset of what CI checks, "Summary" for short descriptions, etc.)
  • the phrasing "take full responsibility for the content" could be memorised by AI. We've realised in mathlib that being more specific is good. The current phrasing is a bit more specific. (I also like your phrasing. Perhaps the superposition of both is best?)

Are there consequences from submitting many low-quality PRs? Do you want to retain the right to ban the contributor/reject all their PRs for a certain amount of time? (Perhaps I'm over-worrying here. But being DDos-ed by AI is not fun, and I don't wish this to anyone, including you.)

(I haven’t had chance to address @Michael Rothgangs comments here yet - hopefully I will next week - though if you are using an AI for physlib can you you for the time being follow what is written at the PR I link to above - as much as possible)

I've been working consistently and intensively with agents (mostly writing systems code) for over 6 months and have the following response:

  1. "small" and "large" are almost useless terms to an agent. They need some notion of scale or calibration. In my experience it's most helpful to think like a lawyer when working with an agent. You don't have to hardcode "small == 32 LoC" and "large == 256 LoC", a qualitative qualifier like a single, one concept lemma is "small" and a theorem adding more than one new lemma is "medium".
  2. It's worth accepting that the policy and agent config guidance, much like any source repo (much like science itself), is never done.
  3. Having feedback from an agent on agent-related matters I find to be incredibly helpful (which I've done below).
  4. Agents love legal theory-type rubrics, so if you can find a way to express the policy in a clear, actionable English algorithm, that will enable the best agentic work. I know it's incredibly vain to cite my own work, but it's the best example of this I can think of right now.
  5. In my experience at Cloudflare, aggressively adopting and articulating agent reviewers turned out to be far more helpful than I would have thought. I don't think it's wrong to allow agents on both sides of the pull request. If we are setting up a policy to allow them on the submitter side, for the sake of scalability while holding reviewer toil ~O(1) very likely means configuring a suite of agentic reviewers as well.
  6. Any code diff is hard biased towards net growth. Even when the intended change is consolidation it's common for the delta to still be a net gain. Agents love to multiply and will kick this trend into a higher power law, so it's worth the effort to constantly remind the agent to strive for a relentless minimalism.

I asked Opus 4.8 (I would have asked Fable because I consider physlib work to be almost always Fable-worthy work but it's not available right now) and it had this response to the proposed policy file [which I generally agree with and have edited]:

Review: AI-POLICY.md (PR #1149)

Framing note: This is a human-facing policy document, not an agent config (AGENTS.md) but the text itself asks agents to read it. [jfindlay edit: separate the human and the agent docs. Create an AGENTS.md for agents. Agents are trained to look for files like this, so it makes it easier for them to find it.]

What's good

  • Type 1 / Type 2 split keyed on "cost of being wrong" — the strongest part of the doc; the right axis for a formal-proof library where a wrong lemma is a long-lived soundness/maintenance liability.
  • "One-look triage" is honest and sets failure-mode expectations up front.
  • must/should defined explicitly (many policies skip this).

Suggested improvements

1. Machine-actionability gaps (inferred)

  • Duplicate / trivial-restatement check is the hardest and most important Type 2 requirement but has no mechanism. Point to concrete tools (exact?, apply?, Loogle, Mathlib search).
  • Linters / Mathlib style — give the actual command(s) or a direct style-guide URL, not a second hop through a README. Each indirection is a silent-failure point.
  • Documentation exemplar (HarmonicOscillator/Basic.lean) — an exemplar isn't a spec; an agent can't tell which properties are normative. Name the salient conventions in a sentence or two.
  • Drift concrete commands couple the doc to current tooling and will drift.

2. Type 1/Type 2 boundary is ambiguous (confirmed)

  • "Golfing a proof" as Type 1 is debatable (compiles-but-fragile golf is a long-lived cost).
  • Author self-classifies, with incentive to claim Type 1 (lower bar). No adjudicator named. Add: "Maintainers may reclassify; if in doubt, treat as Type 2."
  • [jfindlay edit: My intuition is that if you don't give the agent a clear way to distinguish with some confidence (0.7--0.9) which is Type 1 and which is Type 2, you're going to be fighting this battle in every PR.]

3. "Higher standard than human PRs" tension (judgment)

  • The higher bar creates an incentive not to disclose AI use, undercutting the disclosure requirement. Acknowledge the good-faith reliance and state that undisclosed-but-evident AI use is grounds for closing without review.

4. Minor / mechanical (confirmed)

  • Some typos [jfindlay: list omitted]
  • Consider a table of Type 1 vs Type 2 requirement deltas; currently the "(Type 2 PR)" tags are interleaved in a flat list.

5. Possible omissions (inferred)

  • Licensing / provenance — affirm AI output introduces no copyright/license contamination (often a legal must-have for community libraries).
  • AI use in review itself — you ban AI from communicating; clarify whether maintainers may use AI to triage.

Hi,Im still new to lean4 but I wonder if a distributed strategy can help: right now Physlib core maintainers acts as a central authority, thus even rejecting a PR requires energy since it needs to be decided.
Idea is to automate first inspection stage (with logic accepted by Physlib maintainers) so it's ran by each PR submitter, on their equipment or service they use to compute it, load is distributed instead of centralized.

Project already has lean4 comparator
For this to work I assumed something like a Challenge SET must exists that covers all standard logic is proper for any given physics subfield ,
@Justin Findlay Many thanks! My intention is to sit down with this and rewrite things tomorrow.
@Jorge Garcia I think this is the idea of CI and the linters. The better we can make those the easier it will be :). If you have any suggestions here it would be great to hear them!

i believe CI logic tends to be heavy (targeting more often a global scope) while unit testing is meant to target local scopes within the abstractions layers-components on a project. Im not sure what could be the equivalent to unit testing on Physlib, it may be considered redundant but that could be not the case,
Ok, this distinction makes sense. It is probably worth thinking a bit about what we could include as “unit tests”

I've tried to update the AI-policy here Physlib#1149 - not sure it was possible to take everything into account, but hopefully it is an improvement. If anyone has suggested changes - feel free to do on that PR :).
I added a ton of comments and a full split rewrite (sorry). I also think it's useful to include the major points from AI-POLICY.md in the PR message template.
Many thanks @Justin Findlay. I made some changes to your PR, let me know what you think.
@Joseph Tooby-Smith much better. Let me know if you want me to undraft that, or you can appropriate to your branch.
Undraft please - this seems easier :).
Will close my PR.
done
I will wait a day to see if anyone else comments on this, but else this now looks good to me. The relevant PR is now Physlib#1187.

I added three additional rules to prevent some of the most commonly occurring trivial proofs that can be generated by AI agents. My agents pass all Comparator tests after I add these rules, so I believe they are very helpful.

I've updated with another commit. I also added a proscription on scoped variables in hypotheses and statements that are trivially identical. Any other vacuity or circularity gotchas to cover? Does Lean have tooling to detect these kinds of things?

An agent can polyfill reasoning and conclusions but even agents would prefer and agree a closed-form programmatic mechanism is better. Outside of that, clear agent instruction logic is usually sufficient. I have already been deeply impressed at the skill of people contributing to this project writing agent instructions--more than a typical dev or systems engineer.
I'm the author by accident, though, so I'll leave the final sign-off to @Joseph Tooby-Smith.
Thanks both! These look good. I don't know of any direct Lean tooling which detects these automatically, so I think it is good to have them here.

One thing I think it might be worth including (though not sure the best way of stating this), is something along the lines of: 

- make sure that hypothesis are distributed compactly and neatly over new lines.

What I mean is that I often see things like 

def mydef (a : A)
    (b : B)
    (c : C)
    (d : D) : E := e

When 

def mydef (a : A) (b : B) (c :C) (d : D) : E :=
    e

is preferred. Anyone got a better way of phrasing this?
I think it should be fine. We can always adjust it later if it doesn’t work as expected.
I have now merged this! :tada: (feedback still welcome of course)
